title: Make it work for your needs
subtitle: Capture one improvement and the evidence you would use to check it.

coursePath: Turn an idea into a useful result
Decide whether to trust the report
Make it work for your needs

sections.title: Record one opportunity
sections.intro: A reader responsible for Orion wants a report with only Orion’s activity.
sections.html:
The report you handed off includes totals for both projects. Record an Orion-only view as a candidate improvement and keep the original CSV as its input.

Tip: Capture an opportunity in one sentence with the reader, the benefit and one check. For example, “Let the Orion lead generate a report of the four Orion entries and confirm that they total 180 minutes.”
presenterNotes: Keep the opportunity narrow enough to check. Project filtering is proposed behavior.

sections.title: Keep the checked baseline
sections.intro: Use the result you already built and reviewed.
sections.html:
Keep $PRACTICE/activity-report.html, its original six-row CSV and the saved check outcomes. The full report has six entries and 270 minutes.

Optional baseline text output

Use the same course environment and practice path from lesson 2 to print the full report.
presenterNotes: Retain the existing report and saved probe results as the comparison point.

sections.title: Describe the smallest useful change
sections.intro: Write the outcome and its boundaries in plain language.
sections.html:
• Outcome: The reader can ask for a report containing only Orion entries.
  • Preserve: Keep the original CSV, the current checks and the full report when the reader makes no selection.
  • Decide: Agree on how the reader selects a project and what happens if the project name is unknown.
presenterNotes: Leave the interface decision with the learner. Use the current report as the baseline.

sections.title: Write the expected results
sections.intro: Derive both expectations from the original CSV.
sections.html:
• Orion selected: Four entries and 180 minutes (90 + 30 + 45 + 15).
  • No selection: Six entries and 270 minutes.

Use the same entry counts and totals for both text and HTML. These are expectations for the proposed change. The saved baseline checks describe the current program.
presenterNotes: Ask the learner to locate the four Orion rows before evaluating any future implementation.

sections.title: Bring the opportunity to your assistant
sections.intro: Use the saved task path and the new opportunity to prepare a draft.
sections.html:
Start with the generated reply from Come back tomorrow if you are opening a new conversation. Add your opportunity, the two expected results and any open decision.

Review the resulting draft and its checks. Agree on scope and authorize execution as separate steps when you decide to pursue the improvement.

copies.label: change planning prompt
copies.text: Prepare a draft for an Orion-only activity report from the existing six-row CSV. Orion should have four entries and 180 minutes. With no selection, the report should still show six entries and 270 minutes. Keep the input and existing checks intact. Ask me to settle the selection and unknown-project behavior. Show me the draft and checks for review, then stop.

presenterNotes: Reuse the existing context. Treat the new improvement as a separate decision.

sections.title: Try the same idea for Lumen
sections.intro: Optional practice with one independent answer.
sections.html:
Suppose the reader manages Lumen. Use the original CSV to calculate the expected count and total for that project. Keep the full-report expectation intact.

This optional note stays in your browser profile and site.

Check your answer

Lumen has two entries totaling 90 minutes. Development has 60 minutes and Documentation has 30.
presenterNotes: Use the hint after the learner tries the calculation.

check.question: Which evidence would support the proposed Orion filter most directly?

options.text: An unchanged six-row fixture yields four Orion rows and 180 minutes through the new option, while no selection still yields six rows and 270 minutes.
options.feedback: Correct. Those independent outcomes exercise the new selection and preserve the existing baseline. They still need actual execution after implementation.

options.text: The baseline checks prove that a project-filter option already works.
options.feedback: The supplied parser has no project-filter option. Baseline checks cannot establish behavior that was not implemented or exercised.

sections.title: Save the next decision
sections.intro: Leave enough context to pick up the opportunity later.
sections.html:
Keep the opportunity and its two checks with your project handoff. If you return to the saved baseline task, open its current briefing and add the decision you still need to make.

For this example, the next decision is how readers choose a project and how the program handles an unknown name.

Next: Return to Turn an idea into a useful result when you want to frame another opportunity.
presenterNotes: Close with the next decision and the evidence already on hand.
